📕The Tower of Babel in the Digital Age📕

Aleksandar Ivanov

Artificial Intelligence, the Media, and the Restoration of Public Reason

From the Punishment of Misunderstanding to the Promise of Translation

In the biblical account, the Tower of Babel is more than an architectural undertaking. It is an image of humanity’s ambition to turn technical power into a substitute for measure, meaning, and responsibility. People speak one language, coordinate easily, and believe that their shared capacity is sufficient to justify their common purpose. The punishment is not the destruction of the tower, but the collapse of understanding. When words cease to create shared meaning, collective action becomes impossible.

Today, at first sight, technology appears to reverse the myth. Machine translation, automated captions, speech recognition, and large language models are reducing barriers between languages. What once required intermediaries, time, and specialised knowledge can now often be obtained in seconds. Research on multilingual models, including models for programming languages, shows that the transfer of knowledge across languages depends on the structure and distribution of training data. In the early stages, one primary language may dominate, while more language-specific systems may develop later (Chen et al., 2025). Digital translation therefore does not abolish inequality between languages. It can reproduce that inequality in a new, algorithmic form.

This is precisely where the new Tower of Babel begins. It is built not only from servers, chips, and code, but also from the assumption that removing a linguistic barrier automatically creates understanding. Yet understanding is not the same as translation. To translate a sentence is to convey its words; to understand it is to recognise its context, cause, interest, omissions, and consequences. AI can reduce the distance between languages, but it cannot, by itself, overcome the distance between intentions. It may produce a shared vocabulary while we remain enclosed within different political and moral worlds.

Four Authorial Theses as a Single Analytical Arc
This essay does not begin on an empty theoretical foundation. It connects and develops four theses that I previously presented in separate columns: “The Architecture of the Digital Self,” “When We Have All the Answers but No Longer Know What to Ask,” “The Architecture of Critical Thought,” and “The Politics of Multiplication by Zero.” Read together, they form a single analytical arc. The first describes the data-constructed subject upon whom platforms and political campaigns act. The second names the crisis of questioning in an age of instant answers. The third defends analytical depth as a public and educational responsibility. The fourth shows how digital infrastructure can be used to nullify an opponent and manufacture synthetic consent (Ivanov, 2026a; 2026b; 2026c; 2026d).

In “The Architecture of Critical Thought,” this intention is explicit: the columns were not conceived as isolated reactions to daily news, but as a continuous analytical narrative with an educational purpose, grounded in theory, historical parallels, and consistent argumentation (Ivanov, 2026c). The present text should therefore not become a mechanical collection of previously introduced concepts. Its task is to reveal their inner logic: the digital profile determines how a message finds us; the crisis of questioning diminishes our capacity to challenge it; the decline of analytical depth makes the public dependent on ready-made interpretations; and “multiplication by zero” turns disagreement into the erasure of legitimacy.

When Natural Language Becomes a Programming Interface
The most profound change brought by generative AI is not automation alone. It is the democratisation of command. For a long time, programming was the language of a relatively small number of trained people. Today, natural language is becoming an interface through which a user can specify a goal, constraints, format, criteria, and checks. In this sense, the human being truly begins to “programme through language.” Rather than instructing the computer at every step, the user describes an intention and guides the model towards a desired outcome.

Yet the ease of issuing a command creates a dangerous illusion: that the ability to formulate a request is equivalent to the ability to evaluate the answer. It is not. A well-phrased instruction cannot replace conceptual clarity, and a rapid answer cannot replace deep knowledge. A large language model can synthesise, compare, and structure material only within the task we set and the sources available to it. If the question is shallow, the answer may be stylistically brilliant yet epistemically empty. If the concepts are wrongly framed, the system may merely organise the error more elegantly.

I previously formulated this paradox as a condition in which “we have all the answers but no longer know what to ask.” In the column bearing that title, I described the question as one of the most dangerous human freedoms because it subjects the existing order to scrutiny and compels authority to justify itself. From Prometheus and the departure from the cave to the contemporary screen, autonomy begins with the capacity to ask: Why this way? Why not otherwise? Who decides? (Ivanov, 2026b). The digital environment, however, suffers not from a shortage of information but from a shortage of attention, hierarchy, and criteria. Algorithmically curated and emotionally amplified content can create fragmented realities in which factual and manipulative messages become entangled and the common basis for public debate contracts. The problem is not that citizens lack access to facts. The problem is that facts must compete with an endless supply of more striking, personalised, and profitable versions of reality.

Deep knowledge is acquired more slowly. It requires reading, comparison, doubt, a return to sources, and the logical completion of thought. “Common sense” is not an innately infallible instinct, but practical reasoning built upon experience and knowledge. Without foundations, critical thinking easily turns into self-confident disbelief in everything. A society that believes in nothing is not resistant to propaganda. On the contrary, it is ready to believe whatever best corresponds to its fear, anger, or identity.

The Public Sphere Between Argument and the Market for Attention
Democracy is not merely a procedure for counting votes. It presupposes a public sphere in which citizens can obtain relevant information, compare claims, and demand justification from those who hold power. In the Habermasian tradition, legitimacy is created through the public use of reason: argument should take precedence over status, and questions of public interest over private interest. Digital transformation has not destroyed this possibility, but it has radically altered the conditions under which it is realised. Social media have given visibility to previously marginalised voices and created new counter-publics, while simultaneously placing public communication within infrastructures whose business logic is to capture attention and profile users (Staab & Thiel, 2022; Sander, 2025).

In such an environment, information prevails not because it is accurate, but because it is visible, shareable, and emotionally activating. In “The Architecture of the Digital Self,” I introduced the problem of the human data double: political communication no longer addresses only the citizen as a member of the public, but an algorithmically derived profile composed of searches, reactions, habits, contacts, and locations (Ivanov, 2026a). When everyone receives a different version of political reality, the public ceases to be a shared space of disagreement. It becomes a collection of privatised environments of persuasion.

This is the contemporary form of Babel. We do not necessarily speak different languages; rather, we receive the same words in different contexts, with different assumptions and different “evidence.” Here, the “Digital Self” merges with the “politics of multiplication by zero”: personalisation isolates the recipient, while organised digital noise renders the opponent invisible or worthless in advance. In my column on multiplication by zero, I warned that automated accounts, synthetic reactions, and factories of digital noise detach not only the public from reality, but politicians themselves, who may begin to believe the image they have financed (Ivanov, 2026d). Propaganda then ceases to be only a means of manipulating others. It becomes a prison in which power loses the ability to see reality.

The Macedonian Media Landscape: Criticism Must Be Evidence-Based
In Macedonian society, distrust of the media and political elites is not without foundation, but criticism must be more precise than the object it criticises. It is not enough to say that “the media lie” or that every newsroom is a party office. Such a generalisation repeats the logic of propaganda: rather than distinguishing, it nullifies. The stronger thesis is that parts of the media system are exposed to structural pressures that may undermine editorial autonomy: economic vulnerability, opaque ownership, dependence on advertising and public funding, political influence, poor working conditions, and insufficient regulation of the online sphere.

These risks are not merely a matter of perception. Media Pluralism Monitor 2025 includes North Macedonia among the candidate countries assessed in terms of fundamental protection, market plurality, political independence, and the social inclusiveness of the media system. The country report indicates that media freedom must be examined through institutional and market indicators, rather than only through individual scandals (Micevski & Trpevska, 2025). The 2025 shadow report on media freedom likewise presents a mixed picture: legal progress and a decline in physical attacks, but persistent problems involving disinformation, professional standards, political and economic pressure, and regulatory gaps in the online sphere (Epis, Rizaov & Richliev, 2025).

Journalistic consistency is therefore a public value. A journalist has the right to a political and normative orientation. The journalist is not required to have no position, but is required to distinguish fact from commentary, present evidence, show relevant counterarguments, and explain changes in position. Archives enable the public to compare statements over time. If the same commentator applies opposing criteria to an identical event depending on who holds power, the problem is not the journalist’s “humanity,” but an unverifiable and undeclared change of standard.

The archive, however, does not pass judgement by itself. Context may change, new facts may emerge, and a person has the right to revise a position. Democratic responsibility does not require eternal immutability, but reasoned change. The task of AI should therefore not be to hunt for “contradictions” as automatic proof of guilt. It should identify changes, retrieve the sources, and allow the journalist or political actor to explain why the assessment has changed.

Can AI Be More Objective Than a Human Being?
The question of whether AI has room for objectivity is wrongly posed if objectivity is understood as the absence of perspective. Neither a person nor a model sees from “nowhere.” A person is shaped by experience, interest, belonging, and limited knowledge. A model is shaped by data, architecture, developer rules, optimisation criteria, and the sources to which it has access. AI is not a neutral judge. It is a system that may apply a more consistent procedure than a human being, but only if that procedure is clear, verifiable, and open to challenge.

This is precisely why the parallel with a judge’s freedom to assess evidence is useful. Judicial independence does not mean arbitrariness. The assessment of evidence must be reasoned, tied to procedure, and subject to legal review. In the same way, algorithmic analysis can be useful if it reveals its sources, method, degree of confidence, and possible alternative interpretations. If, by contrast, a system provides only a final assessment without showing the path leading to it, automation does not diminish arbitrariness. It merely conceals it behind technical authority.

The scholarly literature already warns of “generative algorithmic epistemic injustice”: AI can amplify manipulative testimony, reproduce distorted representations, marginalise smaller linguistic communities, and distribute access to knowledge unequally. At the same time, the same systems can be designed to detect imbalance, broaden accessibility, and strengthen the integrity of the information ecosystem (Kay, Kasirzadeh & Mohamed, 2024). AI is therefore not a simple solution to risk. It is simultaneously a new source of risk and a new capacity for limiting it.

From Automated Writing to a Public Infrastructure for Verification
The weakest way to introduce AI into journalism is to reduce it to a machine for producing cheap text. The strongest is to build it as an infrastructure for verification. For newsrooms, this would mean systems that automatically connect claims to primary sources; compare budgets, laws, tenders, and statements; flag unsupported figures; detect changes in public positions; transcribe and search lengthy proceedings; and create verifiable timelines. Human beings remain responsible for choosing the subject, making value judgements, protecting sources, and authorising final publication.

Such a system could turn the public archive into an active democratic memory. When a politician makes a new promise, the system could display previous promises, votes, deadlines, and budgetary consequences. When a media outlet publishes a dramatic figure, the tool could compare it with official statistics and methodology. When a sensationalist narrative emerges, AI could map its first appearance, speed of diffusion, and network of repeaters. The result, however, must be an evidence package, not an algorithmic verdict.

In the newsroom, the most important procedure would be “human in the loop”: every automated conclusion should be checked by an accountable person, every correction should remain visible, and every use of generative AI in content of public significance should be transparently disclosed. UNESCO emphasises that AI can increase the efficiency and reach of journalism, while also creating risks of disinformation, hate speech, censorship, and advanced manipulation such as deepfakes. Ethical integration, editorial accountability, and self-regulation are therefore not optional additions, but conditions of legitimate use (UNESCO, 2025).

Six Principles for the Democratic Use of AI in Public Information
If AI is to serve the citizen rather than the ruler, it is not enough for the system to be powerful. It must be institutionally constrained. The first principle is verifiability: factual claims should lead to a source, date, and context. The second is differentiation: the system should clearly distinguish facts, assessments, predictions, and value judgements. The third is pluralism: important contested questions should be presented through the strongest relevant arguments, not through caricatures of the opposing side.

The fourth principle is transparency of automation. Citizens should know when they are interacting with AI, when content has been synthetically generated, and who assumes editorial responsibility. The European regulatory approach already links general-purpose AI systems to documentation, copyright policies, and a public summary of the content used for training; for models presenting systemic risk, it provides additional obligations concerning risk assessment, incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection (European Commission, 2025). This does not guarantee truth, but it creates a trail of accountability.

The fifth principle is protection against the concentration of power. If only the state or a small number of corporations control the models, data, and infrastructure, AI may become a near-perfect instrument of surveillance and targeted influence. Open standards, independent audits, interoperability, and the protection of the public interest in procurement are necessary to prevent a technological monopoly from becoming an epistemic monopoly.

The sixth principle is the right to human challenge. Anyone affected by an automated assessment must be able to understand it, contest it, and request human review. This is especially important for journalistic ratings of “truthfulness,” credibility assessments, and systems capable of affecting reputation. Democratic AI is not AI that never makes mistakes. No such system exists. Democratic AI is AI whose errors can be detected, corrected, and publicly explained.

The Inevitability of Development Does Not Mean the Inevitability of the Outcome
History shows that societies frequently respond with fear to technologies that transform professions and authorities. The typewriter, the computer, the search engine, and the social network all changed the organisation of knowledge and the way people work. But it does not follow that every technological change is progress in itself, or that resistance is always ignorance. The development of AI probably cannot be stopped, but it can be directed. We cannot reasonably return to the pre-digital age, but we can decide which functions to automate, which rights not to delegate, and who will be responsible for harm.

The crucial political error would be to turn the inevitability of technology into the inevitability of a particular institutional model. The future of AI need not belong to a handful of platforms, and public communication need not depend on opaque systems. Public digital infrastructures, university and civic models, independent centres for algorithmic auditing, and newsroom tools aimed not at maximising attention but at increasing verifiability are all possible. Technology opens possibilities; the political community decides which of them will become institutions.

Conclusion: Higher Walls Will Not Save the Tower
The new Tower of Babel is not merely a metaphor for linguistic diversity. It is a metaphor for a society that possesses ever more powerful means of communication while finding it increasingly difficult to create shared meaning. With AI, we can translate almost instantly, search vast archives, and produce persuasive texts at unprecedented speed. But if we lose the capacity to ask good questions, distinguish evidence from impression, and demand consistent criteria, technical connectedness will only accelerate misunderstanding.

Artificial intelligence can contribute to the restoration of public reason if it is used as an instrument of verification, comparison, memory, and explanation. It can help the journalist work faster without becoming more superficial, and help the citizen become better informed without becoming overwhelmed. Yet it cannot replace editorial courage, professional ethics, or civic maturity. Its “objectivity” will not arise from the nature of the machine, but from the quality of the rules, sources, oversight, and possibilities for challenge.

The real choice, therefore, is not between human journalism and machine journalism. It is between opaque automation that concentrates power and verifiable automation that distributes the capacity for oversight. If we choose the second path, AI can become part of democratic infrastructure: not a prophet that proclaims the truth, but an instrument that reveals the evidence; not a censor that closes debate, but an assistant that improves its quality; not a servant of the ruler, but a means by which citizens can once again demand justification from those in power.

Ultimately, we will not save the tower by building it higher. We will save it by subordinating its architecture to a human measure: dignity, freedom, verifiability, and responsibility. Technology will not abolish Babel, but it may help us hear one another again.

Google AI Studio: What It Is, Its Main Tools, and How to Make Money from It

Building an application powered by artificial intelligence has become much easier than it used to be. Instead of writing every line of code manually, you can now describe your application idea in everyday language and use tools such as Google AI Studio to turn that idea into a working prototype that can be developed and published.

However, Google AI Studio is not a magical platform that generates income automatically. Profit comes from using it to create a product or service that solves a real problem for individuals or businesses.

In this article, we will explain what Google AI Studio is, explore its main tools, and discuss practical ways to make money from it.

What Is Google AI Studio?

Google AI Studio is a development environment from Google that allows users to test Gemini models and build applications powered by artificial intelligence.

It can be used to create web applications, AI assistants, file-analysis tools, Android applications, and programs that work with text, images, audio, and video.

Google describes the platform as one of the fastest ways to move from a written prompt to an application powered by Gemini models. Developers can also obtain a Gemini API key through the platform and connect Gemini’s capabilities to external applications.

You do not need to be an expert programmer to get started. However, understanding basic programming and application design will help you identify errors, improve security, and create more professional products.

The Main Tools in Google AI Studio

1. Build Mode for Creating Applications with Prompts

Google AI Studio includes a feature called Build Mode.

Inside Build Mode, you can describe the application you want to create using natural language. For example:

Create an application for managing clinic appointments. It should include a patient registration page, an appointment calendar, and a dashboard showing daily bookings.

After receiving the prompt, the platform generates the application files and displays a live preview next to the code.

You can then request additional changes, such as:

Changing the colors.
Adding a new page.
Creating a login system.
Adding a database.
Fixing a technical error.
Improving the mobile design.

You can start a new project from scratch, modify an existing project from the application gallery, or import a project from GitHub.

How Can You Make Money from Build Mode?

You can build customized applications for small businesses, such as:

Appointment systems for clinics and beauty centers.
Order-management applications for restaurants.
Customer lead-management tools.
Quotation and invoice generators.
Sales and inventory dashboards.
AI assistants that answer customer questions.

You can charge an initial development fee and then collect a monthly payment for maintenance, updates, hosting, and technical support.

2. The Antigravity Coding Agent

Build Mode uses a coding agent known as the Antigravity Agent.

This agent does more than generate a single webpage. It can understand the structure of an entire project, manage multiple files, remember previous changes, and update connected sections of the application.

For example, you could ask it:

Add a subscription system with a free plan and a paid plan. Show each user how many requests they have remaining.

The agent can attempt to update the interface, server, database, and related application logic instead of treating each part separately.

How Can You Profit from It?

You can offer rapid prototype-development services.

Many clients have application ideas but do not want to spend a large amount of money before testing whether the idea will work. You can use Google AI Studio to create an initial version quickly and charge for:

Studying the application idea.
Building the prototype.
Making revisions.
Publishing a test version.
Developing the complete product after the idea has been validated.

This service can be offered to startups, entrepreneurs, agencies, and small-business owners.

3. Creating Full-Stack Web Applications

Google AI Studio is not limited to producing visual interfaces.

It can create web applications with a frontend, usually using React, as well as a server environment based on Node.js.

The server side makes it possible to:

Connect the application to databases.
Use external services.
Install npm packages.
Process data securely.
Protect API keys.
Create user accounts.
Handle payments and subscriptions.
Run automated tasks.

The platform can also work with technologies and frameworks such as React, Angular, and Next.js, depending on the project and available features.

The Business Opportunity

Instead of selling basic websites, you can sell functional systems such as:

Content-management platforms.
Meeting summarization tools.
Customer-message classification systems.
PDF data-extraction applications.
Customer-review analysis dashboards.
Product-description generators.
Customized quotation systems.
Internal company assistants.

The more closely an application is connected to a process that saves time or reduces costs, the more likely a business will be willing to pay for it.

4. Firebase Databases and User Authentication

Google AI Studio can detect when an application needs a database or user accounts and help set up an integration with Firebase after receiving your approval.

This can include:

Cloud Firestore for storing data.
Firebase Authentication for account registration and login.
Google account login.
User-specific records.
Application settings.
Stored conversations and results.

Most commercial applications need to store information such as:

Appointments.
Orders.
Conversations.
Subscriptions.
Analysis results.
Customer records.
Account settings.

How Can You Generate Income from This?

You can use these features to build a subscription-based product, also known as a Micro SaaS.

For example, you could create a tool for online stores that automatically writes and improves product descriptions.

Each store creates an account, receives a limited number of generations per month, and pays for a larger plan when it needs more usage.

Your pricing structure could include:

A limited free trial.
A monthly individual plan.
A higher-priced business plan.
Additional charges for extra usage.
A paid setup and customization service.

This model can generate recurring monthly revenue rather than relying only on one-time projects.

5. Creating Android Applications

Google AI Studio can also help users create native Android applications through natural-language instructions.

It may generate a project using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose and allow users to preview the application in an Android emulator inside the browser.

The application can later be installed on a physical phone or submitted to an internal testing track on Google Play.

However, Android projects may not support all the same server-side features that are available for web applications. Features involving databases, private API keys, Workspace integrations, and server functions may require additional development or a separate backend.

Ideas for Paid Android Applications

You could build:

A student lesson-organizer application.
An AI study assistant.
A personal expense tracker.
A social-media post generator.
A voice-to-summary application.
A revision and quiz application.
A specialized tool for a particular profession.
An application for creating workout plans.
A simple business-management application.

You can monetize an Android application through:

Advertising.
Monthly subscriptions.
In-app purchases.
One-time purchases.
Premium features.
Customized business versions.

6. Working with Text, Images, Audio, and Video

The Gemini API supports different types of content.

It can be used to generate or analyze text, images, audio, video, and other files, depending on the selected model and available features.

This makes it possible to build tools such as:

Product-image analysis applications.
Invoice and receipt readers.
Document data-extraction tools.
Image-description tools for visually impaired users.
Meeting recording analyzers.
Video-review applications.
Complaint and feedback classification systems.
Marketing-image generators.
Short-video production tools.

Google also provides separate AI models and services for image generation, video generation, audio processing, speech, and other media capabilities. Availability and pricing may vary by model, country, and account plan.

How Can You Make Money from These Features?

Create a specialized tool rather than a general-purpose generator.

For example, instead of building a basic image generator, you could create:

An advertising-image generator for restaurants.
A property-marketing tool for real-estate agencies.
A product-image generator for online stores.
A fashion-marketing image tool.
A short-video generator for marketing agencies.
A social-media content system for local businesses.

Specialization makes marketing easier because customers immediately understand what result they will receive.

7. Connecting an Application to Google Search

The Grounding with Google Search feature allows Gemini to use recent information from the internet.

This can help an application provide updated answers and display supporting sources instead of relying only on information previously learned by the model.

This feature could be used to create:

A market-research assistant.
An industry-news monitoring tool.
A competitor-research application.
A product-research assistant.
A sourced report-generation tool.
A research assistant for marketers and writers.

However, Google Search grounding may involve additional usage costs. A single user request may also trigger more than one search operation.

For this reason, developers must monitor consumption carefully when building a paid service.

8. Structured Outputs and Function Calling

Gemini can be instructed to produce information in a structured format, such as JSON with predefined fields.

Instead of receiving an unorganized paragraph, the application could return fields such as:

Customer name.
Phone number.
Request type.
Priority level.
Message summary.
Recommended action.

Gemini models can also work with tools such as:

Google Search.
URL analysis.
Code execution.
File search.
External functions.
Business systems and APIs.

Why Is This Valuable for Businesses?

Structured outputs make it easier to build automation systems, such as:

Reading customer messages and sending them to the correct department.
Extracting invoice information and saving it in a database.
Reviewing résumés based on clearly defined criteria.
Turning written requests into tasks inside a company system.
Reading customer forms and generating reports.
Categorizing support tickets automatically.
Converting emails into organized records.

These services can be more profitable than general content-generation tools because they are directly connected to daily business operations.

The Best Ways to Make Money from Google AI Studio

Method 1: Develop Applications for Clients

Find a company or business owner with a repeated problem, then create a customized tool that solves it.

Your pricing can include:

An initial development fee.
Deployment and integration fees.
A monthly maintenance subscription.
AI usage costs.
Hosting costs.
Charges for additional features.

Do not tell the client that you are selling an “AI application.”

Instead, sell a clear business result, such as:

Reducing the time required to process orders.
Responding to customers more quickly.
Decreasing administrative work.
Producing reports automatically.
Increasing sales leads.
Reducing human errors.

Clients pay for results, not for the name of the technology.

Method 2: Create a Subscription-Based SaaS Product

Build one application that serves multiple users and charge each user a monthly subscription.

Possible ideas include:

A content generator for real-estate offices.
A product-listing assistant.
A customer-review analyzer.
A company file-organizer.
A quiz generator for teachers.
A sales-reporting application.
A conversation-translation platform.
A proposal-writing tool for freelancers.

The advantage of this model is recurring revenue.

However, you will also need to manage:

Marketing.
Customer support.
API costs.
Hosting.
Database usage.
Product updates.
Security.
User retention.

Method 3: Sell Ready-Made Templates

You can create application templates and sell the same template multiple times.

Examples include:

An appointment-system template.
A customer-service assistant template.
A business dashboard template.
A content-management template.
A document-summarization template.
An educational application template.
A sales lead-management template.
A product-description generator template.

After selling the template, you can charge an additional fee for customizing the colors, logo, database, features, and business rules.

Method 4: Offer Business Automation Services

Businesses often have repetitive tasks that consume employees’ time.

You can use Google AI Studio to build tools that reduce this work, such as:

Reading and classifying emails.
Preparing reports.
Organizing documents.
Extracting information from forms.
Summarizing customer conversations.
Processing invoices.
Updating internal databases.
Generating routine business documents.

You can sell this service through a monthly contract that includes monitoring, maintenance, updates, and technical support.

Method 5: Provide Consulting and Training

After gaining experience with the platform, you can offer training sessions to individuals and companies.

Training topics may include:

How to use Google AI Studio.
How to write effective prompts.
How to select the appropriate Gemini model.
How to calculate API costs.
How to protect API keys.
How to turn an idea into a prototype.
How to test application quality.
How to publish a web application.
How to evaluate AI safety and reliability.

You can sell individual sessions, corporate workshops, online courses, or recorded training materials.

A Practical Plan for Building Your First Profitable Project

Start with one industry that you understand, such as:

Clinics.
Restaurants.
Real estate.
Education.
Online stores.
Accounting offices.
Marketing agencies.
Beauty centers.

Speak with potential customers and ask which daily task is repetitive and time-consuming.

Choose only one problem and build a simple prototype that solves it.

Do not spend months adding dozens of features before showing the product to potential customers.

A practical process could look like this:

Select a specific industry.
Identify one measurable problem.
Create a prototype in Build Mode.
Present it to potential customers.
Collect their feedback.
Improve the product.
Set an initial fee and monthly subscription.
Publish the application.
Monitor usage and operating costs.
Add new features only when customers need them.

Your first goal should not be to build a perfect application.

Your first goal should be to find a real customer who is willing to pay.

The Cost of Using Google AI Studio

Some Gemini models can be tested through a free usage tier, while commercial applications with higher usage levels may require billing to be activated.

The cost varies depending on:

The selected Gemini model.
The number of input tokens.
The number of output tokens.
Google Search grounding.
Image generation.
Video generation.
Audio processing.
File storage.
Additional cloud services.

Pricing can change over time, so developers should always review the official Gemini API pricing page before launching a commercial application.

To estimate profit, use the following calculation:

Subscription revenue − Gemini API costs − hosting − database costs − support − marketing expenses = estimated profit

Do not promise unlimited usage before understanding how much each customer consumes.

A safer approach is to give each subscription plan:

A fixed number of requests.
A monthly credit balance.
A document limit.
A storage limit.
Additional paid usage.

This protects your profit margin and prevents a small number of users from creating unexpectedly high costs.

Important Tips Before Selling an Application

Protect Your API Keys

Store API keys on the server side.

Do not place private keys directly inside frontend code, mobile application code, or public repositories.

Exposed API keys can be copied and used by other people, causing unexpected charges or security problems.

Use Proper Deployment

A shared prototype link may be useful for testing, but a commercial product should normally be deployed using a professional hosting environment.

A proper deployment gives you greater control over:

Security.
User access.
Custom domains.
Performance.
Monitoring.
Billing.
Scaling.
Backups.

Review Data and Privacy Policies

Before processing sensitive customer information, review Google’s current data usage and privacy terms.

Avoid entering confidential financial, medical, legal, or customer data until you understand:

How the data is stored.
Whether it is used for model improvement.
Which plan you are using.
Which regional rules apply.
Whether customer consent is required.

Test AI Results

Artificial intelligence can produce incorrect or misleading results.

Always test the application and include human review when it handles:

Financial information.
Medical information.
Legal information.
Hiring decisions.
Important business decisions.
Sensitive customer data.

AI should support important decisions, not make them without proper supervision.

Conclusion

Google AI Studio is more than a place to chat with Gemini.

It is becoming a development environment that can be used to create full-stack web applications, Android applications, document-analysis tools, search-connected assistants, and systems that work with text, images, audio, and video.

The best way to make money from it is not to create another general AI application that looks like dozens of existing products.

Instead, choose a specific industry, identify a repeated problem, and build a tool that saves time, reduces expenses, improves customer service, or increases sales.
